name: Whimsigoth

lead: Whimsigoth is an internet aesthetic that mixes gothic darkness with whimsical, witchy and celestial touches. People adopt it through clothing, jewellery, hair and home decor to give themselves a coherent, atmospheric look.
The term was coined by Evan Collins of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute for home decor and later spread to fashion on TikTok, with fashion and culture outlets covering it from 2022.

paras: Followers combine darker colours and jewel tones with astrology-style prints, flowing layers and witchy accessories. It overlaps with witchcore and cottagecore and draws on 1990s TV and film.
No health risks are specific to the style. As with any trend, items are widely available at varied prices.

chain: Adopt dark jewel tones, celestial motifs and flowing layers
angle.text: Whimsigoth gives a defined palette and set of motifs for assembling outfits and accessories. People use it to look intentional and individual rather than to change their features.

lead: Whimsigoth is an internet aesthetic that blends gothic subculture with whimsical elements. The name, short for whimsical mystical gothic celestial, was coined by architectural designer Evan Collins, co-founder of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, initially for home decor before it spread to fashion on TikTok [1].

It has been described as combining 1970s bohemia with gothic influences of the 1980s and 1990s. Cited influences include Tim Burton films, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, the 1996 Sabrina the Teenage Witch series and the singer Stevie Nicks [1].

People use it as a way of styling themselves: astrological and celestial motifs, darker colours and jewel tones, and witchy details make up its visual vocabulary, and it overlaps with witchcore and cottagecore [1]. Coverage appeared in outlets including Teen Vogue, Glamour and The Guardian between 2022 and 2024 [1].

paras: Collins called the style a postmodern mixture of influences [1]. Its motifs include astrological and celestial imagery, dark gothic or witchy elements, and darker colours alongside jewel tones [1].

Collins first used the term for home decor, and it later moved into fashion as it reached TikTok in the 2020s [1]. Coverage cited by Wikipedia includes Teen Vogue (July 2022), Glamour (September 2022), Alt Press (January 2023), Homes and Gardens (October 2024), Loudwire (November 2024) and The Guardian (December 2024) [1].
